canonical_topic: Standard Market Design: congestion cost allocation
definition: Under FERC's recommended Standard Market Design (SMD), the cost of transmission congestion is charged only to the parties causing or affected by it, rather than spread across all grid users.
core_idea: Both consumers and power producers can pay congestion costs: there is a charge for routing power into a congested high-load area, and a credit for producing power that bypasses congestion; the author frames this as aligning market prices with actual delivery cost, in contrast to price legislation, which the author characterizes as introducing exceptions rather than cost-based pricing.
key_points: SMD assigns congestion costs to the parties actually affected, not the whole grid.
Consumers in congested high-load areas pay a routing charge.
Producers whose power bypasses congestion receive a credit.
Most of the U.S. is moving toward this cost-allocation model.
relationships: Part of the same SMD framework as the remote-generation/line-loss penalty and the LMP concept.
trading_implications: Generators located to relieve congestion are economically favored; there is a market-based incentive to build transmission that reduces congestion.
caveats: The author's framing implies deregulation and cost-reflective pricing are linked, and that legislated pricing is presented as inherently less cost-reflective — this is the author's normative argument, not a neutral technical fact.
